cards.q: What is HTTP and its standard port?
cards.a: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the request/response protocol for the web on TCP 80, and on Cisco gear it also powers the embedded HTTP/HTTPS server for web-based device management; HTTPS (443) replaces it for management.

cards.q: What does an HTTP request/response consist of?
cards.a: A method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), a URI for the resource, a protocol version (HTTP/1.1 with keep-alive by default), headers such as Host and Content-Type, and a body for POST/PUT data.

cards.q: What are the common HTTP methods and key distinction?
cards.a: GET reads a resource, HEAD returns headers only, POST sends data/creates, PUT updates/replaces, and DELETE removes; GET is idempotent/read-only while POST changes state.

cards.q: What do the HTTP status code classes mean?
cards.a: 1xx informational (100 continue), 2xx success (200 OK), 3xx redirect (301/302), 4xx client error (404 not found), and 5xx server error (500/503); the exam-relevant failures are 4xx and 5xx.

cards.q: How does HTTP handle sessions and connections?
cards.a: HTTP is stateless, so sessions rely on cookies/tokens, and keep-alive reuses TCP connections under HTTP/1.1.

cards.q: What commands enable the Cisco embedded HTTP server?
cards.a: ip http server enables web management, ip http port 80 sets the port, ip http authentication local authenticates via the local user database, and ip http access-class restricts access with an ACL; the server also supports GUI and some REST/NetConf APIs.

cards.q: How do HTTP and HTTPS compare for device management?
cards.a: HTTP uses port 80 with no encryption, while HTTPS uses port 443 with TLS; HTTPS is recommended for management, and in modern Cisco defaults HTTP is off.

cards.q: What should you check when a device web page won't load?
cards.a: Whether ip http server is enabled, the URL path (404), authentication config (401/403), an ACL or TCP 80 blocking (access-class), and server stats for keep-alive/proxy slowness.

cards.q: Which protocol should secure Cisco device web management?
cards.a: HTTPS (TCP 443), not plain HTTP; the recommended management stack is ip http server (secure variant) plus authentication and access-class restrictions.
